sections.title: Definition & Pathophysiology
sections.content: Anaphylaxis is an acute, systemic IgE-mediated (or non-IgE-mediated) reaction involving mast cell and basophil activation. Pathophysiology involves the rapid release of mediators: Histamine, Tryptase, Prostaglandin D2, and Leukotrienes, leading to vasodilation, increased capillary permeability, and bronchoconstriction.

rows: Acute onset (min to hrs) with skin/mucosal involvement PLUS respiratory or CV compromise.
2+ of: skin, respiratory, CV, or GI involvement after exposure to likely allergen.
Reduced BP after exposure to known allergen (e.g., <90mmHg systolic or 30% drop).

sections.title: RED FLAGS: Immediate Actions
content: Airway obstruction (stridor, laryngeal edema)
Hypotension/Shock (end-organ hypoperfusion)
Cardiac arrest/Arrhythmia
Refractory bronchospasm
Loss of consciousness

content.explanation: E: Epinephrine (First line!) | P: Position (Supine) | I: IV Fluids | N: Nebulizers | E: Electrolytes | P: Pressors | H: H1/H2 Blockers | R: Refractory checks | I: Intubation if needed | N: Notify team | E: Evaluate vitals

sections.title: Emergency Treatment Algorithm
content: 1. Remove inciting agent immediately.
2. Administer IM Epinephrine (1mg/mL): 0.01 mg/kg (Max 0.5mg in adults) into mid-outer thigh.
3. Position patient supine with legs elevated.
4. High-flow Oxygen (10-15 L/min).
5. Volume expansion with Crystalloids (1-2L isotonic saline).
6. Adjuncts: Albuterol, H1-antagonists (Diphenhydramine 50mg), H2-antagonists (Famotidine), Corticosteroids (Methylprednisolone 125mg).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Do not wait for cutaneous signs (skin symptoms absent in 20% of anaphylaxis).
IM injection in the thigh is superior to SC or subcutaneous injection for rapid absorption.
Biphasic reactions occur in 1-20% of cases; keep patients observed for 4-6 hours.
Beta-blockers can render epinephrine ineffective; consider Glucagon (1-5mg IV) in such patients.
Serum tryptase levels (peak at 60-90 min post-onset) can confirm the diagnosis retrospectively.

sections.title: --- Sub-topics from: Anaphylactic Shock: Ophthalmic Emergency Protocol ---
sections.content: Anaphylaxis is a severe, life-threatening systemic Type I hypersensitivity reaction. In the ophthalmic setting, it is most commonly triggered by intravenous dyes (FFA/ICG), local anesthetics, or latex, requiring immediate recognition and IM Epinephrine administration.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Anaphylaxis is a rapidly developing, multi-systemic immunoglobulin E (IgE)-mediated hypersensitivity reaction. It results from the sudden systemic release of mediators (histamine, tryptase, leukotrienes) from mast cells and basophils. In ophthalmology, it represents the most critical office-based emergency, often occurring within minutes of diagnostic dye injection or anesthetic block.

sections.title: Pathophysiology: The Type I Cascade
content: 1. Sensitization: Initial exposure leads to IgE production by B-cells.
2. Priming: IgE binds to FcεRI receptors on Mast cells and Basophils.
3. Re-exposure: Allergen cross-links IgE on cell surfaces.
4. Degranulation: Massive release of Histamine, Prostaglandin D2, and Leukotrienes.
5. Systemic Effect: Vasodilation, increased capillary permeability, and smooth muscle contraction.

rows: Generalized urticaria, pruritus, flushing, angioedema (lips, tongue, uvula).
Hypotension, tachycardia, arrhythmia, chest pain, cardiac arrest.
Anxiety, 'sense of impending doom', altered mental status, syncope.

sections.title: Ocular Manifestations
content: Severe conjunctival chemosis (often immediate).
Periorbital edema and erythema.
Profuse lacrimation and conjunctival injection.
Sudden vision blurring (due to corneal edema or hypotension).

sections.title: RED FLAGS: Immediate Threats
content: Stridor or hoarseness (Laryngeal edema)
Silent chest on auscultation (Severe bronchospasm)
Systolic BP < 90 mmHg
Rapidly spreading urticaria after IV dye injection
Cyanosis or SpO2 < 92%

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup (Post-Stabilization)
content: 1. Serum Tryptase: Drawn 0.5–3 hours after onset (peak at 1hr).
2. Repeat Tryptase: At 24 hours to establish baseline.
3. Allergy Referral: For skin prick or IgE testing (after 4-6 weeks).
4. Review FFA/ICG logs for lot numbers and dosages.

rows: Bradycardia, pallor, no urticaria, rapid recovery when supine.
Normal BP/O2, tachypnea, carpopedal spasm, no angioedema.
Chest pain, ECG changes, elevated troponins.
No skin changes, history of triggers, slow onset.

sections.title: Management Step-by-Step
content: 1. STOP the offending agent (Disconnect FFA infusion immediately).
2. CALL for help / Activate Emergency Medical Services (EMS).
3. POSITION: Supine with legs elevated (unless respiratory distress predominates).
4. ADRENALINE (Epinephrine): 0.3–0.5 mg IM (1:1000) in the mid-outer thigh.
5. AIRWAY: High-flow Oxygen (15L/min via non-rebreather mask).
6. FLUIDS: Rapid IV bolus of Normal Saline (1-2 Liters).
7. ADJUNCTS: Antihistamines (H1/H2 blockers) and Corticosteroids.

content.explanation: A: Airway, D: Dye Stop, R: Recline/Raise legs, E: Epinephrine IM, N: Normal Saline, A: Antihistamines, L: Lungs (Oxygen/Albuterol), I: IV Access, N: Next dose of Epi if needed.

rows: Skin & subcutaneous tissues only (generalized erythema, urticaria).
Respiratory, cardiovascular, or GI involvement (dyspnea, stridor, nausea).

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for the Ophthalmologist
content: IM Epinephrine is safer and easier than IV Epinephrine for non-coding patients; use the mid-thigh (Vastus Lateralis).
Patients on Beta-blockers may be resistant to Epinephrine; consider Glucagon (1-5mg IV over 5 mins).
Biphasic reactions occur in up to 20% of cases; observe patients for at least 4-12 hours post-event.
Always have a 'Crash Cart' in the FFA suite with up-to-date medications and a portable oxygen tank.
ICG contains Iodine; check for shellfish or iodine allergy before administration.

sections.title: Recent Advances & Landmark Consensus
sections.content: The 2020 World Allergy Organization (WAO) Anaphylaxis Guidance emphasizes that there are no absolute contraindications to Epinephrine in anaphylaxis. Recent studies in 'Ophthalmology' (AAO) suggest that pre-filled auto-injectors (EpiPens) should be accessible in every retina clinic due to their ease of use during high-stress FFA reactions.

sections.title: Complications & Prognosis
content: Hypoxic-Ischemic Encephalopathy (due to prolonged shock).
Myocardial Ischemia / Stress-induced Cardiomyopathy.
Biphasic Reaction (recurrence of symptoms without re-exposure).
Prognosis is excellent if Epinephrine is administered early.
